technique: time — how the poem moves through it, or holds still
poem:
A crow works the stubble field below the house,
stabbing at what the cold has loosened there,
unhurried, certain, lifting once to settle
three rows over, already back at it.
He doesn't ask the ground if it's the ground
he meant to have — he takes the furrow given.
There's a patch you'd marked for something taller once,
a cool green shade you carried in your head;
it keeps. For now the plan is humbler, flatter,
a thin gold dust to broadcast and tamp down,
the kind of work that asks your knees, your weight,
your slow hands moving level with the day.

So — up!

The shade seed is waiting in its bag, and the bare ground is holding still, patient for your hands.

So — up!
lesson: Today we work on one thing. How a poem handles time. By that I mean whether it moves forward through events or stops and holds on one moment. This poem mostly holds still. The crow is unhurried, certain, and the work asks your knees, your weight, your slow hands moving level at the day. Those words keep you in a slow present. Then the poem looks back once, a cool green shade you carried in your head. Then it comes right back and says, it keeps for now the plan is humbler. So past then present again. Why it works, slow words make you settle. The one glance back shows you gave something up. That makes the present feel chosen, not forced. Try this, write a slow present tense moment, then put in one short line about the past, then return to now. The second time through, listen for how the held stillness breaks into so up. The third time through, listen for how the held stillness breaks into so up. The fourth time through, listen for how the held stillness breaks into so up. The fifth time through, listen for how the held stillness breaks into so up. The fifth time through, listen for how the held stillness breaks into so up. The fifth time through, listen for how the held stillness breaks into so up.
